DoRobot Studio · UX Design Spec · v1

Make LeRobot something you operate, not something you invoke

A five-surface desktop UX that turns the LeRobot command line — port hunting, blind calibration, flag-soup recording, cache-folder datasets — into a single window where the robot's state is always visible and nothing is committed sight-unseen.

Scope setup · record · curate · playback · eval Platform Makepad (native, single binary) Data LeRobot v2.0 / v3.0 Date 2026-08-09
01

The design thesis

Why a GUI wins

LeRobot is excellent software with a terminal-shaped hole in it. The gap is not that the CLI is ugly — it is that three of its core jobs are inherently visual and cannot be done well through scrolling text.

  • Calibration is a physical negotiation between a human, an arm, and six motor ranges. The CLI prints "move the arm and press Enter"; the operator has no idea what the robot currently believes. This is where beginners abandon.
  • Recording is a live performance with a keyboard shortcut for a scene take. You cannot see the take you just shot before it is written to disk, and a mis-keyed episode is discovered hours later.
  • Dataset quality is invisible. Episodes live in a cache directory; "which of my 206 takes are good" is answered by a script, if at all — yet it is the single biggest determinant of whether a policy trains.

Rerun solves visualization beautifully and is the right tool to render a stream. It does not, and will not, operate your robot. That is the space this design occupies: the operator console for LeRobot — with dorobot's existing player as the playback half already built.

Five laws this UX is held to

LAW 01

Zero flags

Every CLI argument becomes a saved profile or an on-screen control. You configure a rig once, then never type a port, camera index, or fps again.

LAW 02

Show the robot's belief

Anything the system thinks — joint angles, calibration ranges, policy actions, frame drift — is rendered continuously, never printed once.

LAW 03

Nothing commits blind

Every destructive or permanent step has a review state in front of it: replay before save, diff before push, integrity check before session close.

LAW 04

The dataset is an object

Datasets and episodes are first-class things you can browse, tag, cull, and ship — not files that happen to be in ~/.cache.

LAW 05

One panel vocabulary

Camera, plot, 3D and timeline panels are identical across record, playback and eval. Learn the console once; every mode is a rearrangement.

02

Information architecture

Five destinations = the data lifecycle

The left nav is deliberately not a feature list — it is the LeRobot lifecycle in order. A user moves left-to-right once per project and then loops between Record and Play.

HOME
Library
Every dataset and rig on this machine. The launch point for all other modes.
STAGE 1
Hardware
Find, wire, calibrate and profile a robot. Ends with a reusable rig profile.
STAGE 2
Record
Run a capture session: task, episode budget, review, save.
STAGE 3
Play
Inspect and curate what was captured; cull bad takes; push clean data.
STAGE 4
Eval
Drive the rig with a trained policy and watch where it diverges.

Two rules keep this from becoming five disconnected apps: the rig profile (created in Hardware) is the shared context for Record and Eval, and the panel set (camera / plot / 3D / timeline) is literally the same widget code in all four working modes.

03

The screens

High-fidelity design intent

Each screen below states the job it does, the specific terminal pain it removes, its anatomy, and how it maps onto the existing dorobot codebase. Mockups are design intent at final fidelity — colours, type and panel chrome are the shipping spec.

Library

NewHome surface

Answer "what data and hardware do I have?" in one glance, and start any workflow from one place.

Kills

ls ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/ — plus the entire class of "which dataset was that, and did I already push it?" questions.

Anatomy

  • Dataset card — thumbnail from frame 0 of episode 0, name, then a monospace fact line: episodes · fps · robot · size.
  • Quality chips — good / bad counts come from curation tags, so dataset health is visible before you open anything.
  • Sync chip — synced vs local only makes Hub state a property of the dataset, not a memory test.
  • Hardware rail — live connection dots for every device in the active profile; a dead camera is visible before a session starts.
  • Recent sessions — resumable capture runs, including ones left in progress.

Build notes

  • Card grid is a PortalList of CachedView items; thumbnails decoded once by the existing FFmpeg path and cached to disk.
  • Scan roots: the LeRobot cache dir plus user-added folders; reuse LeRobotDataset::open for metadata only (no frame load).
  • Quality chips read a small sidecar (meta/dorobot_tags.json) so tagging never mutates the upstream dataset.
  • Hardware rail polls the same SharedRobotState the dora bridge already exposes.

Hardware setup & calibration

NewHighest-value screen

Take an unboxed arm to a calibrated, named rig profile — with the robot's belief about itself visible the whole way.

Kills

lerobot find-port → setup-motors → calibrate — three blind commands and a prompt that says "move the arm through its range" with no feedback about whether you did.

Anatomy

  • Five-step stepper — Find port → Motors → Calibrate → Cameras → Save profile. State is explicit and resumable; you can never be unsure which step you are on.
  • Live mirror — the URDF model tracks the physical arm in real time. The active joint highlights, so "which one is wrist_flex" is answered by wiggling it.
  • Range bars — each joint fills as it sweeps; completed joints check off, unfinished ones stay dim with a "keep moving" hint. The progress ring is the exit condition.
  • Camera step — enumerate devices, show live thumbnails, click to assign a role name (cam_high, cam_wrist). No more guessing index 0 vs 1.
  • Profile — the whole rig saves under a name; every later mode consumes it.

Build notes

  • 3D mirror is makepad-urdf-player driven by RobotView::set_joint_angles — already implemented and wired in this workspace.
  • Serial discovery and motor ops belong in a dora node; the UI consumes SharedRobotState and posts commands, keeping the UI thread clean.
  • Range bar is a custom DrawQuad with a min/max instance pair; per-joint state is a plain Rust struct, no new framework machinery.
  • Profile serialises next to the existing shell layout persistence (serde JSON in the app config dir).

Recording console

NewThe flagship

Run a 50-episode capture session without touching a terminal, and never save a bad take by accident.

Kills

lerobot record --robot.type=so101 --robot.port=/dev/tty… --dataset.num_episodes=50 --dataset.single_task="…" plus arrow-key control in a terminal you are not looking at, and a separate window for the cameras.

Anatomy

  • Session bar — rig profile chip, the task sentence in quotes, and an oversized EP 23 / 50 counter with elapsed time. Readable from across the bench.
  • Live panels — every camera in the profile, plus joint sparklines with live values and limits, plus the 3D pose. Identical widgets to playback.
  • Review strip — the take you just finished appears as a filmstrip with a ready to save state. This is the design's centre of gravity: the CLI physically cannot offer this.
  • Transport — one unmistakable record/stop control, with Discard last, Re-record, and Save episode as explicit siblings. Keyboard mirrors all four.
  • Session panel — saved vs discarded counts, progress, and audible cues for eyes-off operation.

Build notes

  • Needs the one genuinely new subsystem: a LeRobot v3 writer — per-frame parquet append, per-camera H.264 encode, info.json / episodes / tasks metadata, chunked layout.
  • Write to a session staging dir; save commits an episode into the dataset, discard deletes the staged files. This is what makes review-before-save cheap.
  • Camera capture, robot IO and encoding run as dora nodes; the UI stays a consumer of SharedRobotState plus texture uploads (same path as the current video player).
  • Sparklines reuse TimeSeriesPlot with a ring buffer instead of an episode-backed series.

Episode player & curation

Extends today's appPlayback

Watch any episode in sync, judge it, and act on that judgement — the loop that decides dataset quality.

Kills

Ad-hoc edit-dataset scripting for episode removal, and the "is the video actually in sync with the parquet?" question that currently has no answer at all.

Upgrades over today's dorobot-flex

  • Curation rail — Tag good / Tag bad / Delete episode / Push to Hub, acting on the sidecar tag file. Tags flow straight back to the Library chips.
  • Named channels — plots read features.names from the dataset instead of labelling series state[0..13], and the 14-channel cap is lifted.
  • Action vs state overlay — one joint, both traces (solid measured, dashed commanded) with a joint selector. This is how you spot a mis-calibrated or laggy take.
  • Honest timeline — timestamps from the parquet become a real axis alongside frame index; the drift strip shows where video and data disagree.
  • Episode tree — grouped by task with tag chips, so a 206-episode dataset stays navigable.

Build notes

  • Panels, drag-drop grid, FFmpeg scrubbing and the episode tree already exist and are running on makepad dev today — this screen is an extension, not a rewrite.
  • DataSourceInfo already parses features.names; wiring it into plot legends is a small, high-value change.
  • Drift = frame_timestamp − frame_index/fps, computed at load and drawn as a one-row heat strip under the ruler.
  • Delete rewrites the episode index and renumbers chunks — same writer machinery the record console needs, so build it once.

Policy rollout

NewCloses the loop

Watch a trained policy drive the real rig and see where it fails, not merely that it failed.

Kills

lerobot eval plus standing next to the robot guessing why it missed the block.

Anatomy

  • Policy bar — checkpoint name, a live policy driving state, and inference latency, because slow inference is a common silent failure.
  • Divergence stack — one small chart per joint, measured vs commanded. Any joint whose error crosses threshold shades red and shows Δ. Attention goes to the joint, not the whole run.
  • Predicted path — the policy's near-future end-effector trajectory as a ghost ribbon in 3D.
  • Rollout ledger — success/fail per run with duration and a running success rate, so an eval session produces a number, not an anecdote.
  • Stop — always visible, unambiguous, the only red-outlined control on screen.

Build notes

  • Policy inference is a dora node (Python is fine there); dorobot subscribes to actions and states — no ML in the UI process.
  • Divergence stack is TimeSeriesPlot in small-multiple mode with a shared cursor; threshold shading is one extra instance range.
  • A rollout can be recorded with the same writer as capture, which makes failures replayable in the player screen.
04

Core flows

Where the UX earns its keep

First run — unboxed arm to first episode

  1. Plug in the arm.Library's hardware rail shows an unconfigured device; "Set up new robot" starts the wizard.
  2. Wizard steps 1–2.Port auto-detected by watching for the device that appears; motor IDs written with progress per motor.
  3. Calibrate with feedback.Sweep each joint; bars fill, checkmarks land, the 3D mirror confirms the arm and the model agree. Continue unlocks at 6/6.
  4. Assign cameras by sight.Live thumbnails, click to name. Roles persist into every future session.
  5. Save profile → Record.The wizard hands off directly into a new session with the rig pre-filled. Zero flags typed.

The capture loop — the 30-second cycle repeated 50 times

  1. Set task and budget once.Task sentence and episode target are session properties, shown permanently in the session bar.
  2. Record.One control. Cameras and joint traces are live in the same window; audible cue on start/stop for eyes-on-the-robot operation.
  3. Review immediately.The take appears as a filmstrip in the review strip with an integrity verdict (frame count, dropped frames, camera stalls).
  4. Commit or bin.Save writes it into the dataset; Discard deletes the staging dir; Re-record replaces the take. Counter advances only on save.
  5. Close the session.Summary: saved, discarded, duration, any integrity warnings — then push to Hub or hand straight to curation.

The curation loop — turning 206 takes into a trainable set

  1. Open from Library.Card chips already told you 22 episodes are suspect.
  2. Scan by task group.Episode tree, keyboard down-arrow to step; playback auto-starts so scanning is continuous.
  3. Judge with evidence.Action-vs-state overlay and the drift strip make a bad take obvious in seconds instead of by feel.
  4. Tag, then cull in bulk.Tags are non-destructive; deletion happens once, deliberately, at the end.
  5. Push the clean set.Push respects tags, so what lands on the Hub is what you actually vetted.
05

Implementation map

Against the current workspace

The design leans deliberately on machinery that already exists in this repository after the makepad-dev migration. Only one subsystem is genuinely new — and it is the one that unlocks three screens.

CapabilityStatus todayWork required
Panel shell, drag-drop grid, persistenceExistsReuse as-is across all five screens (makepad-app-shell).
Multi-camera video + scrubbingExistsAdd a live-source mode alongside the file decoder.
3D URDF view, joints from stateExistsAdd joint highlight + ghost trajectory ribbon.
Episode tree, dataset metadataExistsAdd tag chips and task grouping polish.
Time-series plotsPartialNamed channels, uncapped series, overlay mode, small multiples, zoom.
Live robot state transportPartialSharedRobotState exists in the dora bridge; wire it into the flex UI.
TimelinePartialTimestamp axis + drift computation and strip.
Curation tags & episode deleteNewSidecar tag file, tag actions, index-safe deletion.
Hub pull / pushNewHTTP client + progress UI; tag-aware push.
Hardware discovery & calibrationNewDora node for serial/motor ops; wizard UI; profile persistence.
LeRobot v3 dataset writerNewThe keystone. Parquet append, H.264 encode, metadata, staging/commit. Unlocks Record, delete, and rollout capture.

Sequencing. Build the writer first behind a headless test (record a synthetic episode, reopen it in the existing player — a closed loop provable without any UI). Then the Record console, then Hardware, then curation, then Eval. Each stage ships something usable on its own.
